newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian banks combine to fight foreign newcomes.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian banks combine to fight foreign newcomes.

text.p: Slovenia's banks are struggling to stay afloat in an increasingly overcrowded industry and are expected to embrace each other in a wave of mergers over the next few years.

The prospect of the tiny Alpine republic opening its doors to international banks is exacerbating the need for domestic operators to clamp down on costs and prepare themselves for stiff competition, analysts say.

Currently 28 banks operate in Slovenia, which has a population of just two million. The top banks -- Nova Ljubljanska banka, Nova Kreditna Banka Maribor and SKB -- control more than half of the market.
Mergers have aready begun. On Thursday, the second-largest bank SKB said it would buy a 51 percent stake in UBK to form the country's third banking group.

"The number of domestic bank groups will fall to about seven in a period of some four years when the market will be entirely open for foreign banks," said Aleksander Simon, an analyst at state-owned Nova Ljubljanska Banka, the largest bank in the former Yugoslav republic.

A new bank bill, which is expected to be adopted by parliament by the end of this year, would enable foreign banks to open branches in Slovenia. At present, foreign banks can only set up subsidiaries, requiring substantial capital outlay.
According to the bill, foreign banks would have to apply for a Bank of Slovenia licence before establishing a branch.
But if Slovenia becomes a full member of the European Union, which it hopes to achieve around 2001, such a licence would no longer be needed.

"The forming of new banking groups is in line with Slovenia's approaching (membership of) the European Union," said Peter Stanovnik, head of the Institute of Economic Research at Ljubljana University.
"It is a positive development because it will reduce the cost of bank services and interest rates," Stanovnik added.
"Slovenian banks are three times less productive than foreign banks," Ivan Nerad, SKB's chief executive told a news conference called to announce the merger plans.
"Our link-up (with UBK) will have a positive effect for both banks. It will reduce costs especially concerning investment in development," Nerad added.
Some smaller bank mergers took place in January when Celje took over Noricum and bought into Hmezad, while Nova Ljubljanska banka heads a group which includes a number of its subsidiaries.
Dolenjska bank has also said it was considering a merger this year, but has declined to reveal any details.
